rows.line: Sarah slides a stairlift brochure across the table.
It's just a stairlift, Mum. Just look at it.
I know what it is.
I watched you come down those stairs backwards.
Then don't watch.
Somebody has to. You're 71. Some days you don't even come downstairs. Dad's bringing your tea up on a tray.
I've done the physio, Sarah. The painkillers. The injections. I've got a drawer full of braces upstairs, and the last one slid down around my ankle by the evening.
So let them put the stairlift in.
A stairlift is how it starts.
How what starts?
Margaret doesn't answer.
Do you ever think about which one of us goes first?
Frank.
If it's me... who gets you down the stairs?
A long silence.
Go to sleep, love.
She lies there with her eyes open.

rows.dir: in her wedding dress, holding out her hands
rows.line: Grandma, you promised. When I was little, you said you'd dance at my wedding.
I know I did, sweetheart. I'll watch from here.
Emily's smile drops. She goes back to the dance floor, where a woman in her seventies is dancing like she's forty.
Is that Barbara out there? Your cousin Barbara?
She's 74.
I thought her knees were bone on bone.
They are. I always thought hers weren't as bad as mine.
Barbara, staying for the week, watches Margaret line up two pills, a tube of gel, a knee brace and an ice pack.
You've done this every morning since I got here. Two pills, the gel, the brace and an ice pack.
For eleven years.
Can I show you something?
Barbara pulls up her trouser leg. A small black strap sits just under her kneecap.
It's called Stryde. I had it on at the wedding. All night.
That little thing? Barbara, that can't possibly work on knees like mine.
That's exactly what I said. Last winter I was sleeping on my sofa because I couldn't get up my own stairs.
Every brace you've ever bought was made to keep you comfortable while your knee got worse. A sleeve just squeezes the knee. A brace just stops it going sideways. Does your knee hurt going sideways?
No.
It hurts coming down the stairs. Put your finger just under your kneecap. Two centimetres down. Press in. Feel that band?
Yes.
That's the tendon. Every step you take lands right there. Seventeen times your bodyweight goes through it. Every stride.
Barbara, my knees are bone on bone. There's nothing left in there.
Mine too. This doesn't put anything back. Nothing can, and anyone who tells you otherwise is lying to you. I'm 74, Margaret. I haven't got time to lie to you.
Then what does it do?

It changes where the weight lands. It sits just under the kneecap, right on that band. There's a silicone pad on the inside. The pad presses on that one spot, instead of spreading the pressure around the whole knee like a sleeve does. It catches the weight and moves it off the worn part, before it gets to the joint.
They measured it. Thirty four percent less strain, every step.

Bone on bone, arthritis, worn cartilage, meniscus. Whichever one your doctor said it was, that's the spot taking the weight. Every brace and every injection you've had was aimed at the whole knee. Not that spot. That's why nothing worked.
Your arthritis will still be there. The weight just won't be landing where it hurts.
It'll slip. They all slip.

It's adjustable, and it doesn't go over the joint, so there's nothing to bunch up or roll down. Ten seconds to put on. It sits flat under your trousers, and you forget it's there. They spent three years building it with orthopaedic surgeons. Over two hundred thousand people wear one.
I can't try another thing that doesn't work, Barbara. I can't get my hopes up again.

rows.dir: putting a strap in her hand
rows.line: Then don't get your hopes up. Just put it on and walk down the stairs. And keep your hand on the rail. I'm not crazy.
Margaret stands at the top, gripping the post. Barbara waits at the bottom.
I can't, Barbara. I haven't come down these forwards in two years.
Hand on the rail. One step. That's all I'm asking.
Margaret takes the first step. Slowly. She waits for her knee to give.
Feel that under the kneecap? That's the weight going somewhere else.
The second step. The third. Her eyes fill.
Barbara... I'm not gripping it.
I know, love. Keep coming.
She comes the rest of the way down. Both feet. Forwards. At the bottom she puts her hand over her mouth and weeps.
I can't believe it. I can't believe it.
Barbara holds her.
Well, don't just stand there. Put the kettle on.
Margaret laughs through her tears.
Your new X-ray looks exactly like the old one, Margaret. Bone on bone, both knees.
I know.
So how did you just walk in here like that?
Margaret pulls up her trouser leg.
That makes sense. It's moving the weight off the worn part. Keep wearing it.
I wasn't planning on taking it off.
Margaret comes in with two bags of shopping. Frank is in the hall with his coat half on.
I was just coming to look for you. You were gone a long time.
I know.
Where did you go?
Into town.
You walked into town? That's two miles.
Each way.
Frank looks at her for a long moment.
I called the stairlift man.
Frank...
I told him not to come. (his voice goes) All those nights I lay there thinking, if it's me that goes first...
Then I'll manage the stairs.
Sarah follows her mother up the stairs with her arms out, the way she always does.
Slowly, Mum. I'm right behind you.
Margaret goes up forwards at a normal pace, hand resting on the rail. At the top, she turns around.
You can put your arms down now, love.
Sarah is halfway up with her arms still out. She slowly lowers them.
Mum... when did that happen?
Six weeks ago. Barbara happened.
What does that even mean?
It sits on the tendon under my kneecap and moves the weight off the worn part. My knees are still 71. It's not because the arthritis has gone. It's because the weight isn't landing where it hurts.
Later. Music on the kitchen radio.
Grandma. You still owe me a dance.
I always keep my promises.
Margaret takes her hands. They dance slowly around the kitchen, Margaret in her slippers. Sarah watches from the doorway, laughing and crying at the same time.
Joan, it's me. I've found something for your knees.
Oh, Margaret. Not another one.

That's exactly what I said. It's called Stryde. Barbara gave me one. Get it from their website, the real one. There are copies out there. It's two for one right now, so you can do both knees. And if it doesn't work, you get your money back. Sixty days, and you keep the straps.
Well. What have I got to lose?
Nothing. Come over on Sunday. You're walking up my stairs on your own.

hooks.name: A · "Get away"
hooks.vis: Cool, grey grade. Extreme close-up: her knee trembles as she lowers herself backwards down the stairs, leading with the same foot, knuckles white on the banister. Sarah drops her shopping in the hall and runs up. Close-up: Margaret yanks her arm out of Sarah's hand. Sarah freezes. Close-up: Margaret turns her face to the wall with her chin shaking. She isn't angry, she's ashamed. Cut to a black screen with white text: 6 weeks ago

lines.line: Mum! Your knee! Here, let me help you.
No! I can do this. Get away from me!
I know. Please don't watch me.

hooks.name: B · "Seventy-one!"
hooks.vis: Warm, bright grade. A busy station staircase at rush hour, with rails on both sides and one down the middle. Close-up: two women in their late 40s, each gripping a side rail, stiff-kneed, one step at a time. Margaret (71, work lanyard, handbag) comes down the middle almost running, her hand skimming the centre rail. Extreme close-up: her knees move easily, and a small black strap shows just under the kneecap below a cropped trouser hem. She slips between the two women, both heads turn, and she's gone. Cut to a black screen with white text: 6 weeks ago

lines.line: Excuse me! Sorry, love, I'm late for work!

lines.dir: from the bottom, not looking back

hooks.name: C · The floor
hooks.vis: Cool, grey grade. Close-up: a mug slides off the counter. Margaret bends for it. Extreme close-up: her right knee buckles sideways and she shouts as she drops. Frank (70s, cardigan) gets down slowly, puts his arm under hers and pulls. Close-up: his arms shake, and she doesn't move. Wide: they end up sitting on the floor together, backs against the cupboards. Cut to a black screen with white text: 6 weeks ago

lines.line: I've got you. Give me your arm.
Stop, Frank. You'll hurt your back.
I'm not leaving you on the floor.
